messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alejandro had always been drawn to the fast-paced world of tech startups, but his latest stint as a product manager in Caracas had taken an unexpected turn. As protests against the government escalated into violent clashes, Alejandro found himself caught in the crossfire. He remembered the sound of gunfire and shattering glass, the smell of smoke and sweat, and the feeling of his heart racing as he sprinted for cover. In the months that followed, Alejandro struggled to shake off the sense of unease that lingered long after he'd left the war-torn streets behind. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, as if it was waiting for the next explosion or gunshot. He would startle at unexpected movement nearby, his heart racing like it had that day in Caracas. "I'm always on edge," he told himself, "like I'm just one wrong move away from disaster." This sense of hypervigilance had become his new normal, and Alejandro couldn't seem to turn it off. As the days turned into weeks, Alejandro began to develop coping mechanisms to deal with this perpetual state of alertness. He started checking his body constantly for signs of danger or injury, scrutinizing every ache and pain as if it might be a warning sign of something more sinister. "What if I'm hurt and don't even know it?" he'd think to himself, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. This obsessive monitoring only seemed to heighten his sense of threat, making him feel like he was walking on eggshells all the time. In an attempt to calm his frazzled nerves, Alejandro turned to self-harm as a way to release some of the pent-up anxiety that had been building inside him. He'd hurt himself physically, just enough to distract himself from the constant feeling of being "on guard." It was a twisted logic, he knew, but it seemed to work – at least in the short term. The physical pain would momentarily eclipse the emotional turmoil, giving him a fleeting sense of relief. But this self-destructive behavior only served to reinforce Alejandro's deep-seated conviction that he was in grave danger all the time. "I'm not okay," he'd tell himself, "and I need to keep proving it to myself." This toxic cycle had become a vicious feedback loop: his body on high alert → his desperate attempts to calm himself through self-harm → an even greater sense of threat and vulnerability. As Alejandro navigated the sterile office spaces of Silicon Valley, he felt like an outsider – a stranger in a strange land. His colleagues seemed oblivious to the constant danger lurking around every corner, their smiles and laughter grating on his nerves like fingernails on a chalkboard. "Don't they get it?" he'd think to himself, frustration simmering just below the surface. "We're all just one misstep away from disaster." Alejandro's product management skills were still top-notch, but his growing isolation had begun to affect his work performance – and his overall well-being. It was only when Alejandro's best friend staged an intervention, expressing deep concern about his self-destructive behavior and growing reclusiveness, that he realized the gravity of his situation. "I'm scared for you, man," his friend said, eyes filled with worry. "You need help." For Alejandro, this wake-up call marked a turning point: maybe it was time to confront the demons head-on, rather than trying to outrun them forever.
